attributes.title: Level 6

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the backgroundImage asset to display the project’s color palette on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might a color palette be displayed in the background image on screen?

❓ What do you notice about the colors in the project’s color palette?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In this activity, the ninja will be creating a sprite pack, or a collection of sprites of different kinds that can show different perspectives of a sprite included. A sprite pack tends to have a unifying theme and is made for other users to use.

💡 The color palette will be used to design each of the sprite images included in the sprite pack. Having the color palette on screen helps the user identify the unifying colors and theme across the images.
steps.instructions:
Display the project’s color palette on screen, which will be used to create each sprite image!


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen. 


Open the backgroundImage asset and notice that there are 8 different colored squares on the top left of the image. These represent the colors that will be used in each sprite image for the project to create a unified sprite pack. Notice the background color is not in the color palette; this is to create contrast so the images in the sprite pack do not blend into the background.


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add code to display the backgroundImage asset on screen.


Click ▶ to see the color palette background appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add an xOffset value (15) with a spacing value (20), multiplied by the counter variable i like this: (15 + (20 * i)), to set each Player sprite’s x-position?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about each of the Player image assets?

❓ What other sprites do you think might be added to the sprite pack?

❓ What values might you use to offset the Player sprite images from the left side of the screen and to space out each image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to open each Player image asset. Have them notice the similarities and differences between each image and how they show a different perspective, matching the direction they’re facing. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to identify the colors from the color palette used in each image and have them brainstorm what other sprite images might be paired with the Player. 

💡 Remind the ninja to use the documentation if they need help storing the Player image assets in the array, or placing them on screen.
steps.instructions:
Display the Player sprite images in a row on screen!


Open the Assets menu again, then click on each Player image, and notice how each asset’s name matches the direction that the sprite is facing. 


Return to the JavaScript editor, then declare a playerImages array. Store the 4 Player image assets inside.


Below, add a for loop that will run while the counter variable is less than the length of the playerImages array. Create a Player sprite each time the loop runs, using the counter variable to select a different image from the playerImages array index.


Set the x-position of the Player sprites by adding a value to offset the left side of the screen with the spacing between each sprite, multiplied by the counter variable. Set the sprites to appear in a row just below the color palette.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprites appear on screen. Notice how the color palette is used in each image.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place the Obstacle sprite on the same row as the Player sprite images?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you think the theme of the sprite pack might be?

❓ What do you notice about the bulldozerImage asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the color palette, Player images, and Obstacle image to think through the theme of the sprite pack. In the next steps, the ninja will create additional sprites to match the construction-themed sprite pack.

💡 Have the ninja open the bulldozerImage asset and notice the colors from the color palette that are used in the image, where highlights and shadows are applied, and how the outline is used to define the shape.
steps.instructions:
Display the Obstacle sprite image on screen!


Open the Assets menu again, then click on the Obstacle sprite image and consider the theme of the project. 


Return to the JavaScript editor, then create an Obstacle sprite using the bulldozerImage asset. Set the sprite to appear on the same row as the Player sprites.


Click ▶ to see the Obstacle sprite appear on screen. Notice how the color palette is used in the image.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you draw a construction-themed Enemy sprite image, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of image might you create for the Enemy sprite?

❓ What color(s) from the project’s color palette might you use as the base for the Enemy sprite?

❓ Where might pixels be erased to remove any jaggies from the Enemy sprite image outline?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to think outside the box when designing their Enemy sprite. Prompt them to consider the theme of the sprite pack, based on the Player and Obstacle images, to brainstorm an idea for the Enemy sprite. 

💡 Remind the ninja that a jaggy is a break in a smooth line in an image. Pixel art lines are formed by connecting “steps” of pixels. To create a smooth straight line, there should be the same number of pixels on each step of the line.
steps.instructions:
Add an Enemy sprite to the sprite pack!


Consider what type of sprite might be used as an Enemy in this construction-themed project.


Create a new image asset. Begin by drawing an outline of the image, then use the erase tool to remove any jaggies from the outline. 


Use 1 or 2 colors from the project’s color palette to add a base color to the image.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add highlights and shadows to the Enemy sprite image, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might highlights and shadows be added to the Enemy sprite image to add depth?

❓ What other finishing touches might be added to the Enemy sprite image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that they should only use colors from the project’s color palette to add highlights and shadows.

💡 Remind the ninja that a highlight is the point of an image where the light hits the object. Highlights should be added to a pixel art image in a color lighter than the base color. The highlight should be placed on the same side as the light source. 

💡 Remind the ninja that a shadow adds depth to a pixel art image, making it appear as if it’s three dimensional, rather than just a flat object on screen. Shadows should be drawn in a color darker than the base color and should be placed on the opposite side as the light source, showing how the light shines across the object.
steps.instructions:
Add additional features to the Enemy sprite image!


Consider where the light source in the image is, then use a light color to add highlights and a dark color to add shadows to the image. Add polish and any other final details to the Enemy sprite image to make it look complete.


Return to the JavaScript editor and display the Enemy sprite below the Player and Obstacle sprites on screen.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprite on screen. Compare its appearance to the other sprites and the color palette to make sure it fits with the overall theme of the project.

steps.hints: ❓Did you create a construction-themed Projectile sprite image, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of image might you create for the Projectile sprite? What colors might be included?

❓ How does the Projectile sprite compare with the Player, Obstacle, and Enemy sprites?

❓ What size might the Projectile image be? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to think outside the box when designing their Projectile sprite. Prompt them to think about the theme of the sprite pack, based on the Player, Obstacle, and Enemy images, to brainstorm an idea for the Projectile sprite. 

💡 It might be useful for the ninja to explore premade Projectile sprite images in MakeCode’s library. Have the ninja notice that Projectiles are often smaller images, typically 8x8 pixels instead of 16x16. Have the ninja tinker with the size of the Projectile image as they are creating.
steps.instructions:
Add a Projectile sprite to the sprite pack!


Consider what type of sprite might be used as a Projectile in this construction-themed project.


Create a new image asset. Begin by drawing an outline of the image, then remove any jaggies. Fill the outline with base colors from the project’s color palette.


Consider where the light source in the image is, then add highlights and shadows to the image. Add any other final details to the sprite.


Return to the JavaScript editor and display the Projectile sprite on the same row as the Enemy sprite.


Click ▶ to see the Projectile sprite on screen. Compare its appearance to the other sprites and the color palette to make sure it fits with the project theme.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the project’s color palette to design the 2 Collectible sprite images, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of images might you create for the Collectible  sprites? What colors might be included?

❓ How do the Collectible sprites compare with the Player, Obstacle, Enemy and Projectile sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to think outside the box when designing their Collectible sprites. Prompt them to think about the theme of the sprite pack, based on the Player , Obstacle, Enemy and Projectile images, to brainstorm an idea for the Projectile sprite. 

💡 As the ninja is designing their Collectible sprite images, they may want to refer back to the color palette and notice what colors have not been used as much in the previous images.
steps.instructions:
Add 2 Collectible sprites to the sprite pack!


Consider what type of sprites might be collected in this construction-themed project.


Create a new image asset. Begin by drawing an outline of the image, then remove any jaggies. Fill the outline with base colors from the project’s color palette.


Consider where the light source in the image is, then add highlights and shadows to the image. Add any other final details to the sprite.


Repeat this process with the second Collectible sprite image.


Return to the JavaScript editor and display the Collectible sprites on the same row as the Enemy and Projectile sprites.


Click ▶ to see the Collectible sprites on screen. Compare its appearance to the other sprites and the color palette to make sure it fits with the project theme.

steps.hints: ❓Did you design a new image asset to complete the construction-themed sprite pack?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What kind of sprite is missing from the sprite pack?

❓ What colors have not been used from the color palette yet?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja brainstorm what else they might include in the sprite pack. Prompt the ninja to think through how each sprite might be used in a project in order to help them come up with another sprite image to include.
steps.instructions:
Add an additional sprite to complete the sprite pack!


Look at the existing sprites on screen and consider what other sprites are missing from this construction-themed sprite pack, that might be needed when used in a project. 


Create a new image asset. Draw the outline, then fill it in with base colors. Add highlights, shadows, and polish to add depth to the image.


Return to the JavaScript editor and display the sprite on screen.


Click ▶ to see the new sprite appear on screen! Compare its appearance to the other sprites and the color palette to make sure it fits with the project theme.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you review the sprite pack to make sure each image uses the project’s color palette and matches its theme?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the sprite pack appear on screen? Is there anything out of place or missing?

❓ How might the sprite pack be used in a project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to make sure there is a unifying theme and color palette across the sprite images. If something looks off or out of place, encourage the ninja to return to the image and tinker with it so that it makes more sense in the sprite pack.
steps.instructions:
Finalize the sprite pack!


Look over each of the sprite images on screen. Does each sprite image use colors from the project’s color palette? Does each sprite image fit the construction theme of the project? What else might be added or changed?


Add any other finishing touches to complete the sprite pack!


Click ▶ to see the finalized sprite images on screen!

subgroups.title: Create a Color Palette for a Sprite Pack
subgroups.introduction: Design a construction-themed sprite pack that uses a specific color palette to create original image assets for different sprite kinds.

validationItems.text: Display the background image that shows the project’s color palette on screen.
Place the 4 Player sprite images on screen.
Place the Obstacle sprite image on screen.
Place the custom image assets on screen to complete the sprite pack

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 6 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about creating images that show multiple perspectives of the same sprite and themed sprite packs for projects. You’ll be able to take the strategies you learn in this level to create detailed assets in future projects! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 6:

badges.title: Package Deal
badges.description: Create a sprite pack that includes different sprite kinds and different perspectives of those sprites, to be used in a project.

badges.title: Covering All My Bases
badges.description: Create pixel art images that show multiple points of view for a sprite: forward, backward, left, and right.

badges.title: Group by Theme
badges.description: Use a specific color palette and theme to create a sprite pack of different sprite kinds.

badges.title: The Gang’s All Here!
badges.description: Create a sprite pack of original pixel art images that includes Player, Collectible, Goal, Enemy, and Projectile sprites.
